gh issue create --milestone "v1.1 Backlog" --label bug --label priority/P2 --title "Frontend OIDC: hardcoded offline_access scope likely breaks Cognito sign-in (invalid_scope)" --body "Found in the pre-apply review of the AWS track. \`frontend/src/auth/authClient.ts\` always requests \`scope = openid profile email offline_access [apiScope]\`. \`offline_access\` is not a Cognito scope (system scopes are \`openid\`, \`email\`, \`phone\`, \`profile\`, \`aws.cognito.signin.user.admin\`) and can't be added to \`allowed_oauth_scopes\`.

Per the [authorize-endpoint docs](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/cognito/latest/developerguide/authorization-endpoint.html), an unknown/invalid scope returns \`error=invalid_scope\` to the redirect URI (the docs also say unassociated scopes are \"ignored at runtime\" — the two statements conflict, and community reports of \`invalid_scope\` for un-enabled scopes are common, e.g. rancher/rancher#54127). If it errors, sign-in is dead on Cognito; if ignored, it works (Cognito issues refresh tokens on the code grant regardless of \`offline_access\`).

Needs a live check against a real pool (#953 rule). If it errors: make the scope list provider-tolerant — e.g. an optional \`DATAQ_AUTH_SCOPE\` runtime override, or drop \`offline_access\` when the discovery document's \`scopes_supported\` omits it." 2>&1 | tail -1; gh issue create --milestone "v1.1 Backlog" --label bug --label priority/P2 --title "AWS: github-deploy IAM policy's ecs:cluster condition denies RegisterTaskDefinition" --body "Found in the pre-apply review of \`deploy/terraform/aws/github_oidc.tf\` (#1342). The \`EcsDeploy\` statement puts \`ecs:RegisterTaskDefinition\`, \`ecs:DescribeTaskDefinition\` (and \`ecs:DescribeTasks\`) under an \`ArnEquals\` condition on \`ecs:cluster\`. Those actions don't populate the \`ecs:cluster\` condition key (task definitions aren't cluster-scoped), so the condition evaluates against a missing key → **implicit deny**. The future \`deploy-aws.yml\` would fail at its first \`aws ecs register-task-definition\`.

Fix: split the statement — cluster-scoped actions (\`UpdateService\`, \`RunTask\`, \`DescribeServices\`) keep the \`ecs:cluster\` condition; \`RegisterTaskDefinition\`/\`DescribeTaskDefinition\` move to their own statement (resource-level \`*\`, no cluster condition — that's the best available scoping for the task-definition action family). Harmless to fix before first apply; must be fixed before the deploy workflow exists." 2>&1 | tail -1

The frontend target group health-checks \`/healthz\`, which the nginx image **proxies to the api** (\`nginx.conf.template\` \`location = /healthz\`). So if the api is down, the ALB marks the (perfectly healthy) frontend targets unhealthy and ECS kills/replaces frontend tasks in a loop — masking the real failure and taking the static SPA (and its error page) down with it.

Also relevant to first bring-up: until \`deploy-aws.yml\` exists and rolls a current image, the services start on the create-time defaults \`backend :v10\` / \`frontend :v2\` — and \`:v10\` (2026-06-29) predates both \`OidcBearerScheme\` and \`SECRET_STORE=aws_secrets_manager\`, so the api/worker will crash-loop and the frontend will flap on this health check from the first minute after apply.

Fix options: health-check a static nginx path (e.g. \`/\` serving index.html, or a new nginx-local \`/livez\` stanza) so frontend health means \"nginx is up\", and keep api health observable via its own service/logs — or accept + document the coupling." 2>&1 | tail -1

content.text:
Review done — **verdict: NOT clean, so per your "iff all looks good" gate I did not run `tofu plan`/`apply`.** Five findings filed as issues #1345–#1349. Here's the full report.

## What I reviewed

All three merged changes end-to-end: [#1337](https://github.com/TheurgicDuke771/DataQ/pull/1337)'s `AwsSecretsManagerStore` ([secrets.py](backend/app/core/secrets.py)), [#1340](https://github.com/TheurgicDuke771/DataQ/pull/1340)'s `OidcBearerScheme` + config + MCP mode ladder ([auth.py](backend/app/core/auth.py), [config.py](backend/app/core/config.py), [mcp/auth.py](backend/app/mcp/auth.py)), and all 17 files of [#1342](https://github.com/TheurgicDuke771/DataQ/pull/1342)'s [deploy/terraform/aws/](deploy/terraform/aws/) — cross-checked against the frontend's actual runtime auth contract ([authClient.ts](frontend/src/auth/authClient.ts), [config.ts](frontend/src/auth/config.ts), [nginx.conf.template](frontend/nginx.conf.template)), the Azure stack's container commands, and AWS's own documentation for the claims I couldn't settle from code.

## Blockers (why the apply is off)

**1. Cognito rejects HTTP callback URLs — the "HTTP-only ALB, no domain" and "Cognito" decisions are mutually incompatible ([#1345](https://github.com/TheurgicDuke771/DataQ/issues/1345), P1).** AWS requires redirect URIs to be HTTPS except `http://localhost`. [cognito.tf](deploy/terraform/aws/cognito.tf) registers `http://<alb-dns>/auth/callback`, so the apply is expected to fail at the user-pool client — and even if it created, sign-in could never complete. Same issue also covers a second bug hiding behind it: the SPA's redirect URI is `${origin}/`, never `/auth/callback`, so the registered path is wrong regardless. This needs **your decision**: cheapest fix without buying a domain is CloudFront in front of the ALB (free default `*.cloudfront.net` HTTPS cert); the alternative is a domain + ACM. I didn't pick one because it un-locks a decision you locked.

**2. Cognito access tokens carry no `email` claim ([#1346](https://github.com/TheurgicDuke771/DataQ/issues/1346), P1).** `_extract_oidc_claims` reads `email` off the bearer, but the SPA sends the *access* token, and Cognito access tokens have no email/name. Every user would provision with `email=""` — admin allowlist dead, and the **second** user to sign in hits the unique lower-email index and is permanently 409'd. The #1340 tests hand-built claims *with* email present — the exact fixture-encodes-our-model shape the project's #953 rule warns about. Suggested fix in the issue: fall back to the standard `userinfo` endpoint (provider-neutral).

**3. The SPA hardcodes `offline_access` in its scope request ([#1347](https://github.com/TheurgicDuke771/DataQ/issues/1347), P2).** Not a Cognito scope; AWS docs say unknown scopes return `error=invalid_scope` at the authorize endpoint (with some conflicting "ignored at runtime" wording — needs the live check, but it's a real provider-neutrality gap either way).

**4. The GitHub-deploy IAM policy denies `RegisterTaskDefinition` ([#1348](https://github.com/TheurgicDuke771/DataQ/issues/1348), P2).** The `ecs:cluster` `ArnEquals` condition covers actions that never populate that condition key, which evaluates to an implicit deny — the future `deploy-aws.yml` would fail at its first task-definition registration. Mechanical fix (split the statement); should land before first apply.

**5. First-boot reality + health-check coupling ([#1349](https://github.com/TheurgicDuke771/DataQ/issues/1349), P3).** Until `deploy-aws.yml` exists, apply brings services up on the create-time defaults `:v10`/`:v2` — and backend `:v10` (June) predates both `OidcBearerScheme` and `SECRET_STORE=aws_secrets_manager`, so api/worker would crash-loop from minute one. Compounding it, the ALB health-checks frontend `/healthz`, which nginx *proxies to the api* — an api outage recycles healthy frontend tasks.

## What checked out (verified, not just skimmed)

- **Provider-neutrality of the backend**: `OidcBearerScheme` is genuinely generic — OIDC discovery + JWKS via PyJWT, no vendor SDK; alg pinned to RS256 (no alg-confusion), `kid` required, issuer verified, fail-closed on JWKS outage with a single refresh-retry, mutual exclusion with Azure enforced at boot, MCP mode ladder mirrors REST exactly. No Entra claims leak into route code. The one provider-aware line (Cognito `client_id`-vs-`aud`) is documented and flagged for live verification, as recorded.
- **Secrets architecture**: clean two-owner split — infra bootstrap secrets readable only by the *execution* role, the app's runtime prefix (`dataq/*`) granted only to task roles; the store's `rstrip("/")` + forced-`/` join lines up exactly with the IAM resource pattern; `ListSecrets`' unscopeable grant is correctly narrowed client-side with `startswith`. Outage vs not-found exception discipline preserved.
- **Security posture elsewhere**: no credentials in any tracked file; state encryption (pbkdf2/AES-GCM) with the passphrase handled correctly; `.gitignore` covers tfstate/tfvars/plans; GitHub OIDC federation with exact repo+environment subject (no stored keys); RDS `publicly_accessible=false` + TLS, ElastiCache TLS + auth token with the `/`-`"`-`@` exclusion handled; SGs are least-privilege (the task self-ingress already narrowed to 8000 by the pre-merge review); Redis pinned to 7.1 (consistent with the redis-8-is-new-attack-surface rule); Cognito password policy is strong.
- **Verified-benign**: worker/migrate commands match the Azure stack byte-for-byte; `rediss://` without explicit `ssl_cert_reqs` defaults to CERT_REQUIRED in kombu/redis-py, which works against ElastiCache's valid cert; frontend's unset `DATAQ_AUTH_API_SCOPE` falls back to the image's empty-string default; `assign_public_ip=true` is the documented no-NAT tradeoff with SGs doing the gating.

## Recommended order from here

1. You decide the HTTPS approach (CloudFront vs. domain+ACM) — everything in #1345 hangs on the final public origin.
2. Fix #1345/#1348 in the TF stack, #1346 (+#1347 verification hook) in code — normal PR flow.
3. Then apply, build `deploy-aws.yml`, roll current images, and live-verify the two Cognito accommodations against a real pool.

I've updated nothing in the repo itself — findings are all filed. Sources for the AWS-behavior claims: [Cognito authorize endpoint](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/cognito/latest/developerguide/authorization-endpoint.html) (HTTPS-only redirect URIs, `invalid_scope`), [CreateUserPoolClient](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/cognito-user-identity-pools/latest/APIReference/API_CreateUserPoolClient.html), [rancher/rancher#54127](https://github.com/rancher/rancher/issues/54127) (invalid_scope in practice).

    public_jwk["kid"] = "test-key"
    public_jwk["use"] = "sig"
    return private_key, public_jwk

    """Resolve `jwks_uri` from an OIDC issuer's discovery document.

    Synchronous and shared by both callers that need it: `OidcBearerScheme.
    load_config` below (wrapped in `asyncio.to_thread` — it must not block the
    event loop) and `mcp.auth.build_auth_provider` (genuinely synchronous —
    fastmcp's auth provider is built at **module import time**, before any
    async startup hook exists to call into). One implementation, not a
    sync/async pair that could quietly drift apart.

    response = httpx.get(f"{issuer.rstrip('/')}/.well-known/openid-configuration", timeout=timeout)

    Synchronous and shared by every caller that needs a discovery field:
    `OidcBearerScheme.load_config` below (wrapped in `asyncio.to_thread` — it
    must not block the event loop), `mcp.auth.build_auth_provider` (genuinely
    synchronous — fastmcp's auth provider is built at **module import time**,
    before any async startup hook exists to call into), and `fetch_userinfo`
    (#1346). One implementation, not a sync/async pair that could quietly
    drift apart.
    """
    response = httpx.get(f"{issuer.rstrip('/')}/.well-known/openid-configuration", timeout=timeout)
    response.raise_for_status()

# ── userinfo fallback (#1346) ────────────────────────────────────────────────
#
# Cognito access tokens carry no `email`/`name` (only sub/client_id/scope/…),
# so identity claims a token omits are resolved from the issuer's standard
# `userinfo` endpoint instead — provider-neutral: any token that already embeds
# `email` (Azure AD, Keycloak defaults, …) never triggers the round-trip.
#
# The cache is keyed by the token's SHA-256 (never the raw bearer — it must not
# sit in a long-lived dict a heap dump could read) and bounded: userinfo is one
# extra HTTP call per token per TTL, not per request.

_USERINFO_TTL_SECONDS = 300.0
_USERINFO_CACHE_MAX = 1024
_userinfo_cache: dict[str, tuple[float, dict[str, Any]]] = {}


def _userinfo_cache_get(token: str) -> dict[str, Any] | None:
    entry = _userinfo_cache.get(hashlib.sha256(token.encode()).hexdigest())
    if entry is None or entry[0] < time.monotonic():
        return None
    return entry[1]


def _userinfo_cache_put(token: str, claims: dict[str, Any]) -> None:
    now = time.monotonic()
    if len(_userinfo_cache) >= _USERINFO_CACHE_MAX:
        for key in [k for k, (expiry, _) in _userinfo_cache.items() if expiry < now]:
            del _userinfo_cache[key]
        while len(_userinfo_cache) >= _USERINFO_CACHE_MAX:
            # Still full after dropping expired entries: evict oldest-inserted.
            del _userinfo_cache[next(iter(_userinfo_cache))]
    _userinfo_cache[hashlib.sha256(token.encode()).hexdigest()] = (
        now + _USERINFO_TTL_SECONDS,
        claims,
    )


def _merge_userinfo(claims: dict[str, Any], userinfo: dict[str, Any]) -> dict[str, Any] | None:
    """`claims` with `email`/`name` filled from `userinfo`, or None on sub mismatch.

    OIDC Core §5.3.2: the client MUST verify the userinfo `sub` matches the
    token's — a mismatch means the response describes someone else (an IdP bug
    or a swapped response) and the sign-in must fail rather than mint a user
    row from mixed identities.
    """
    if userinfo.get("sub") != claims.get("sub"):
        return None
    for claim in ("email", "name"):
        if not claims.get(claim) and userinfo.get(claim):
            claims[claim] = userinfo[claim]
    return claims


def fetch_userinfo(issuer: str, token: str, *, timeout: float = 5.0) -> dict[str, Any] | None:
    """The issuer's userinfo response for `token` — sync, for `mcp.auth` (#1346).

    Returns None when the provider publishes no `userinfo_endpoint` (it is
    RECOMMENDED, not required — the caller proceeds with whatever the token
    carried). Raises `httpx.HTTPError` on an outage: an unreachable endpoint is
    an outage to surface, never an empty identity (the ADR 0039 decision 6
    lesson applied to auth). The REST path (`OidcBearerScheme._verify`) does
    the same fetch through its own async client; both share the TTL cache.
    """
    cached = _userinfo_cache_get(token)
    if cached is not None:
        return cached
    endpoint = discover_oidc_config(issuer, timeout=timeout).get("userinfo_endpoint")
    if not endpoint:
        return None
    response = httpx.get(
        str(endpoint), headers={"Authorization": f"Bearer {token}"}, timeout=timeout
    )
    response.raise_for_status()
    userinfo: dict[str, Any] = response.json()
    _userinfo_cache_put(token, userinfo)
    return userinfo

if token is not None:
        claims: dict[str, Any] = token.claims or {}
        # PAT path (ADR 0026): the verifier already resolved (and last-used-
        # stamped) the owning user; load it by id — no upsert, the user exists.
        pat_user_id = claims.get(PAT_USER_CLAIM)
        if pat_user_id:
            user = session.get(User, pat_user_id)
            if user is None:  # revoked/deleted between verify and tool call
                raise McpAuthError("could not resolve the API key's user")
            return user
        settings = get_settings()
        mode = mcp_auth_mode(settings)
        if mode == "generic_oidc":
            # `sub` — the RFC 7519 REQUIRED subject claim — not Azure's `oid`.
            # No guest-user policy here: that concept is Azure B2B-specific, and
            # the generic REST validator (`core.auth.OidcBearerScheme`) applies
            # none either.
            subject = claims.get("sub")
            if subject:
                email = str(claims.get("email") or "")
                name = claims.get("name")
                return _upsert_user(
                    session,
                    aad_object_id=str(subject),
                    email=email,
                    display_name=str(name) if name is not None else None,
                    oidc_issuer=settings.oidc_issuer,
                )
        else:
            # Mirror the REST validator's guest policy: reject Azure AD guests
            # (B2B / external) unless explicitly allowed, so /mcp can't accept
            # an identity the REST API would 403. The JWTVerifier already
            # validated signature / issuer / audience / scope; this is the
            # tenant-membership policy on top.
            if not settings.azure_allow_guest_users and is_guest(claims):
                raise McpAuthError("guest users are not permitted")
            # `oid` (the stable directory object id) is mandatory, exactly as
            # the REST resolver treats it — never fall back to `sub` (a per-app
            # pairwise pseudonym), which would key a divergent / duplicate
            # users row.
            aad_oid = claims.get("oid")
            if aad_oid:
                email = str(
                    claims.get("preferred_username")

# ── OidcBearerScheme: userinfo fallback (#1346) ──────────────────────────────
#
# Cognito access tokens carry no `email`/`name`; the scheme resolves them from
# the issuer's userinfo endpoint. These tests drive the REAL verify path with
# signed tokens — only HTTP is mocked.


@pytest.fixture(autouse=True)
def _clear_userinfo_cache() -> Any:
    auth_mod._userinfo_cache.clear()
    yield
    auth_mod._userinfo_cache.clear()


class _UserinfoTransport:
    """Serves /jwks.json + /userinfo, counting userinfo hits (cache assertions)."""

    def __init__(self, jwks: dict[str, Any], userinfo: dict[str, Any] | int) -> None:
        self.jwks = jwks
        self.userinfo = userinfo  # dict → 200 body; int → that status code
        self.userinfo_calls = 0
        self.userinfo_auth_headers: list[str] = []

    def handler(self, request: httpx.Request) -> httpx.Response:
        if request.url.path == "/jwks.json":
            return httpx.Response(200, json=self.jwks)
        if request.url.path == "/userinfo":
            self.userinfo_calls += 1
            self.userinfo_auth_headers.append(request.headers.get("Authorization", ""))
            if isinstance(self.userinfo, int):
                return httpx.Response(self.userinfo)
            return httpx.Response(200, json=self.userinfo)
        return httpx.Response(404)


async def _scheme_with_userinfo(
    monkeypatch: pytest.MonkeyPatch,
    issuer: str,
    jwks: dict[str, Any],
    userinfo: dict[str, Any] | int,
) -> tuple[auth_mod.OidcBearerScheme, _UserinfoTransport]:
    scheme = auth_mod.OidcBearerScheme(issuer=issuer, audience="dataq-client-id")
    monkeypatch.setattr(
        httpx,
        "get",
        lambda url, timeout: httpx.Response(
            200,
            json={"jwks_uri": f"{issuer}/jwks.json", "userinfo_endpoint": f"{issuer}/userinfo"},
            request=httpx.Request("GET", url),
        ),
    )
    transport = _UserinfoTransport(jwks, userinfo)
    monkeypatch.setattr(
        scheme, "_client", httpx.AsyncClient(transport=httpx.MockTransport(transport.handler))
    )
    await scheme.load_config()
    return scheme, transport


def _cognito_access_token(private_key: rsa.RSAPrivateKey, issuer: str) -> str:
    """The real Cognito access-token claim shape: client_id, no aud, NO email."""
    return _sign(

        {
            "sub": "cognito-sub-1",
            "iss": issuer,
            "client_id": "dataq-client-id",

# DataQ frontend image — build the Vite SPA, serve the static dist via nginx.
# Build context = frontend/ :  docker build -f frontend/Dockerfile frontend/
#
# ONE generic image, nothing baked in (ADR 0028): no cloud, no secret, no
# auth-bypass. Auth config is injected at RUNTIME — nginx serves /config.js from
# the DATAQ_AUTH_* env below (envsubst at startup), and the SPA reads it before
# the bundle runs. So the same image serves the eval stack (DATAQ_AUTH_MODE=bypass)
# and a real deployment (DATAQ_AUTH_MODE=oidc + authority/clientId/scope) — set the
# env at `docker run`, no rebuild. Replaces the #472 two-image (:latest/:dev) split.
#
# The deploy workflow builds + pushes this image and rolls the `dataq-app-frontend`
# Container App (ADR 0028 §5 cutover — the Static Web App is gone; SWA couldn't
# inject runtime config). See deploy/terraform/azure/frontend.tf.

# Pin the build stage to the native BUILD platform (amd64 on CI runners) even for
# an arm64 target image: a Vite SPA compiles to architecture-independent static
# assets, so there's no reason to run `pnpm build` under arm64 QEMU emulation — it
# only made the multi-arch publish pathologically slow / flaky (12min good case →
# 45min stall, #512). buildx cross-builds: this stage runs native, and only the
# tiny per-arch nginx `serve` stage below is built for each target platform, with
# the arch-independent dist COPYed in. $BUILDPLATFORM is a buildx-predefined arg.
FROM --platform=$BUILDPLATFORM node:22-alpine AS build
WORKDIR /app
RUN corepack enable

COPY package.json pnpm-lock.yaml ./
RUN pnpm install --frozen-lockfile

COPY . .
RUN pnpm build

FROM nginx:1.27-alpine AS serve
# Link the GHCR package to this repo (shows under the repo's Packages, lets the
# repo's Actions GITHUB_TOKEN push it, and inherits anonymous-pull visibility —
# ADR 0023, mirrors backend/Dockerfile).
LABEL org.opencontainers.image.source="https://github.com/TheurgicDuke771/DataQ"
LABEL org.opencontainers.image.description="DataQ frontend (React SPA served by nginx)"
LABEL org.opencontainers.image.licenses="MIT"
COPY --from=build /app/dist /usr/share/nginx/html
# Template (not a static conf): the nginx entrypoint envsubst's it at startup so
# the API upstream + auth config are runtime-configurable.
COPY nginx.conf.template /etc/nginx/templates/default.conf.template
# Opt into the nginx image's built-in resolver detection: its
# 15-local-resolvers.envsh only exports ${NGINX_LOCAL_RESOLVERS} (the
# /etc/resolv.conf nameservers, used by the proxy `resolver` directive) when this
# flag is set. Cloud-neutral (ADR 0028) — no resolver IP baked in; works in
# compose (127.0.0.11) and ACA/K8s (cluster DNS) alike.
ENV NGINX_ENTRYPOINT_LOCAL_RESOLVERS=1

# bypass needs an explicit DATAQ_AUTH_MODE=bypass. DATAQ_API_UPSTREAM defaults to

    DATAQ_AUTH_MODE="" \
    DATAQ_AUTH_AUTHORITY="" \
    DATAQ_AUTH_CLIENT_ID="" \
    DATAQ_AUTH_API_SCOPE=""
EXPOSE 8080

69	  // bypass even if VITE_AUTH_DEV_BYPASS=true were baked in. The image path never
70	  // reaches here (nginx injects window.__DATAQ_CONFIG__).
71	  const bypass = import.meta.env.DEV && import.meta.env.VITE_AUTH_DEV_BYPASS === 'true';
72	  // `pnpm dev` against a locally-running OTP backend. Explicit opt-in only — an
73	  // unrecognised value falls through to the OIDC/unconfigured branches rather
74	  // than being coerced into a mode. Not DEV-gated like bypass, because unlike
75	  // bypass this mode *is* a real authenticator: turning it on in a production
76	  // bundle grants nothing without a mailbox and a server-side allowlist.
77	  const otp = import.meta.env.VITE_AUTH_MODE === 'otp';
78	  return {
79	    // OTP is checked BEFORE bypass (#1150). `VITE_AUTH_DEV_BYPASS=true` is the
80	    // long-standing dev default and lives in the compose file; an explicitly
81	    // named mode has to win over a leftover boolean, or the local stack would
82	    // render "no sign-in at all" while its backend was serving email codes —
83	    // the split-brain the two-selector contract exists to prevent. Safe
84	    // direction: this can only ever REPLACE a bypass with a real authenticator.
85	    mode: otp ? 'otp' : bypass ? 'bypass' : tenantId && clientId ? 'oidc' : undefined,
86	    authority: tenantId ? `https://login.microsoftonline.com/${tenantId}/v2.0` : undefined,
87	    clientId: clientId || undefined,
88	    apiScope: apiClientId ? `api://${apiClientId}/${scope}` : undefined,
89	  };
90	}
91	
92	// The injected runtime config wins; the build-time env is the dev-only fallback
93	// used only when no /config.js was served (i.e. `pnpm dev`).
94	const injected = typeof window !== 'undefined' ? window.__DATAQ_CONFIG__?.auth : undefined;
95	const cfg: DataqAuthConfig = injected ?? fromBuildEnv();
96	
97	export const authConfig = {
98	  authority: cfg.authority,
99	  clientId: cfg.clientId,
100	  apiScope: cfg.apiScope,
101	} as const;
102	
103	export const authMode: AuthMode = (() => {
104	  // Fail-closed: bypass and otp ONLY on their explicit flag, never inferred.
105	  if (cfg.mode === 'bypass') return 'dev_bypass';
106	  // Checked before the OIDC branch so a deployment that leaves stale
107	  // authority/clientId values behind while switching to `otp` gets the mode it
108	  // asked for, rather than silently continuing to render an IdP redirect.
109	  if (cfg.mode === 'otp') return 'otp';
110	  if (cfg.authority && cfg.clientId) return 'real';
111	  return 'unconfigured';
112	})();

119	  unconfigured: 'Not configured',
120	};

# Amazon Cognito — the OIDC identity provider for this deployment, validated
# by the backend's new provider-neutral `OidcBearerScheme` (ADR 0026
# amendment) instead of the Azure-only `fastapi_azure_auth` path. No code
# change needed here beyond what already shipped: this stack only needs to
# set OIDC_ISSUER + OIDC_AUDIENCE (backend) and the DATAQ_AUTH_* runtime
# contract (frontend, already generic per ADR 0028).
#
# Known open item (tracked, not silently assumed correct): Cognito's OAuth
# ACCESS token carries `client_id`, not the standard `aud` claim.
# OidcBearerScheme already accommodates this — see its docstring — but the
# accommodation needs confirming against a REAL token from this pool once
# it exists (this codebase's "#953 rule": driver/third-party-boundary claims
# need a live check, not just a spec read).

resource "aws_cognito_user_pool" "app" {
  name = "dataq-app"

  auto_verified_attributes = ["email"]

  password_policy {
    minimum_length    = 12
    require_lowercase = true
    require_numbers   = true
    require_symbols   = true
    require_uppercase = true
  }

  username_attributes = ["email"]

  tags = { Name = "dataq-app-cognito" }
}

# Domain prefix must be globally unique across all of Cognito — the random
# suffix (shared with other globally-unique-name resources in this stack)
# avoids a name collision on a common word like "dataq".
resource "aws_cognito_user_pool_domain" "app" {
  domain       = "dataq-app-${random_string.suffix.result}"
  user_pool_id = aws_cognito_user_pool.app.id
}

# Public SPA client — no secret (a browser can't hold one), matching how the
# frontend's oidc-client-ts uses Authorization Code + PKCE (authClient.ts).
resource "aws_cognito_user_pool_client" "spa" {
  name         = "dataq-app-spa"
  user_pool_id = aws_cognito_user_pool.app.id

  generate_secret = false

  allowed_oauth_flows_user_pool_client = true
  allowed_oauth_flows                  = ["code"]
  allowed_oauth_scopes                 = ["openid", "email", "profile"]
  supported_identity_providers         = ["COGNITO"]

  callback_urls = ["${local.frontend_url}${var.cognito_callback_path}"]
  logout_urls   = [local.frontend_url]

  # Access tokens are short-lived (1h) by default; the SPA relies on
  # oidc-client-ts's silent-renew via the refresh token, same pattern Azure
  # uses (authClient.ts requests offline_access).
  explicit_auth_flows = ["ALLOW_USER_SRP_AUTH", "ALLOW_REFRESH_TOKEN_AUTH"]
}

locals {
  # The standard OIDC issuer URL Cognito publishes discovery + JWKS under —
  # exactly what OidcBearerScheme's `discover_jwks_uri` GETs
  # `{issuer}/.well-known/openid-configuration` from.
  cognito_issuer = "https://cognito-idp.${var.aws_region}.amazonaws.com/${aws_cognito_user_pool.app.id}"
}

data "aws_iam_policy_document" "github_deploy" {
  # Two statements, split by whether the action populates the `ecs:cluster`
  # condition key (#1348). Task-definition actions are not cluster-scoped and
  # never set the key, so putting them under the ArnEquals condition made the
  # condition evaluate against a MISSING key — an implicit deny that would
  # have failed the workflow's first `register-task-definition`.
  statement {
    sid = "EcsDeployClusterScoped"
    actions = [
      "ecs:UpdateService",
      "ecs:DescribeServices",
      "ecs:RunTask",
      "ecs:DescribeTasks",
    ]
    resources = ["*"]
    condition {
      test     = "ArnEquals"
      variable = "ecs:cluster"
      values   = [aws_ecs_cluster.app.arn]
    }
  }

  statement {
    sid = "EcsTaskDefinitions"
    actions = [
      "ecs:RegisterTaskDefinition",
      "ecs:DescribeTaskDefinition",
    ]
    # `*` is the best available scoping: the task-definition action family
    # supports no resource-level restriction (registration creates a NEW
    # revision ARN). The blast radius stays contained by the PassTaskRoles
    # statement below — a registered definition is inert unless it can be run,
    # and running it needs a role this policy will only pass for this stack's
    # own task/execution roles, on this stack's cluster.
    resources = ["*"]
  }

# DataQ on AWS — Terraform (OpenTofu) runbook

A second, parallel deployment of DataQ (Azure stays the deployed prod — see
`deploy/terraform/azure/`), into a fresh, dedicated AWS account. Unlike the
Azure stack, nothing here is shared with another stack: this account exists
only for this deployment.

## What it creates

| Resource | Purpose |
|---|---|
| VPC, 2 public subnets, IGW, route table | Networking. No NAT Gateway (decision: public-subnets-no-NAT, ~$33/mo saved — ECS tasks get no public inbound access, only the ALB→frontend path is internet-reachable) |
| `aws_ecs_cluster.app` + 3 Fargate services (api, worker, frontend) + 1 task def (migrate) | The app itself. api is internal-only (Cloud Map DNS `api.dataq.local`); frontend is the sole public surface (behind the ALB); worker runs embedded celery-beat, `desired_count=1` always (cannot scale to zero) |
| `aws_lb.app` (ALB, HTTP-only) | Public ingress → frontend target group only |
| `aws_db_instance.app` (RDS Postgres, `db.t4g.micro`) | The app's own database — this stack creates it directly (no shared-server bootstrap dance like the Azure stack, since this account is dedicated) |
| `aws_elasticache_replication_group.app` (`cache.t4g.micro`, TLS + auth token) | Celery broker + rate-limit store |
| `aws_cognito_user_pool.app` + SPA client | OIDC identity provider, validated by the backend's provider-neutral `OidcBearerScheme` (ADR 0026 amendment) — not Azure AD |
| `aws_secretsmanager_secret.*` (2, infra-owned) + IAM grants | `database-url`/`redis-url` (infra-owned, referenced by ARN in task defs) + the app's own runtime grant under `AWS_SECRETS_MANAGER_PREFIX` (`SECRET_STORE=aws_secrets_manager`) |
| `aws_iam_openid_connect_provider.github` + `aws_iam_role.github_deploy` | GitHub Actions → AWS auth for the Deploy workflow, OIDC federation, no stored access keys |
| CloudWatch Log Groups (4) | Container logs. No APM/tracing wired up yet — the OTel core is vendor-neutral but the exporter shipped so far is Azure-only |

## Prerequisites

- **OpenTofu** (`tofu`), not Terraform — same ADR 0024 rationale as the Azure stack.
- **AWS CLI credentials** for a **scoped IAM user**, never root. This repo's own bring-up used `AWS_PROFILE=dataq-deploy` (set as the default in the operator's shell) — see the session notes for the IAM bootstrap steps (create user, attach a policy, remove root's access keys/login session).
- A **GitHub repo** with Actions enabled (for the OIDC federation to have something to trust).
- Nothing else pre-exists — this stack creates its own VPC, database, cache, etc. from scratch, unlike the Azure stack's shared-resource dependencies.

## Apply

```bash
cd deploy/terraform/aws
tofu init
tofu plan -input=false -out=tfplan \
  -var="app_db_password=REDACTED -c 'import secrets; print(secrets.token_urlsafe(32))')" \
  # state_encryption_passphrase comes from your terraform.tfvars — see terraform.tfvars.example
tofu apply -input=false tfplan
```

**Cost starts here.** `tofu apply` creates real, billable AWS resources (Fargate, RDS, ElastiCache, ALB). Review the plan before applying. See the root-level deployment plan (in the session that built this stack) for the cost breakdown against the AWS free-tier credit.

## After apply — wire the Deploy workflow

```bash
tofu output -raw github_deploy_role_arn   # → repo secret AWS_DEPLOY_ROLE_ARN
tofu output -raw ecs_cluster_name         # → repo variable ECS_CLUSTER
tofu output -raw frontend_url             # → sanity-check reachability
```

```bash
gh secret set AWS_DEPLOY_ROLE_ARN --body "$(tofu output -raw github_deploy_role_arn)"
gh variable set ECS_CLUSTER --body "$(tofu output -raw ecs_cluster_name)"
gh variable set AWS_REGION --body "$(tofu output -raw -json | jq -r .aws_region.value 2>/dev/null || echo us-east-2)"
```

A companion `.github/workflows/deploy-aws.yml` (not yet built) will use these
to `aws-actions/configure-aws-credentials` via OIDC, then run the same
build→push(GHCR)→migrate(RunTask, poll-to-terminal)→`ecs update-service`
sequence the Azure `deploy.yml` runs, adapted to the AWS CLI equivalents.

## State encryption

Same discipline as the Azure stack (`versions.tf`'s `encryption {}` block):
the local state holds the generated RDS/ElastiCache passwords in plaintext
without it. `state_encryption_passphrase` is a **data-at-rest key**, not a
credential — it cannot be revoked or re-minted, and losing it makes
`terraform.tfstate` permanently unreadable. Keep a second copy off this
machine. A wrong/missing passphrase fails closed
(`cipher: message authentication failed`) without corrupting the file.

## Verify

```bash
# Confirm exactly what got created, tagged for this stack:
aws resourcegroupstaggingapi get-resources \
  --tag-filters Key=Purpose,Values=dataq-app-aws

# Reachability (through the frontend — the sole public surface):
curl -s "$(tofu output -raw frontend_url)/healthz"
```

Then in a browser: sign in through Cognito end-to-end, confirm `/api` and
`/mcp` return 401 unauthenticated without a credential, and run one real
suite against a live datasource to confirm the worker path.

## Known gaps in this pass (deliberately deferred, not silently skipped)

- No custom domain / HTTPS — ALB DNS name, HTTP-only. Add Route53 + ACM + an
  HTTPS listener once a domain is chosen.
- No private-subnet/NAT hardening — see `main.tf`'s decision note.
- No `.github/workflows/deploy-aws.yml` yet — this stack only provisions the
  infra the workflow will drive.
- The Cognito `client_id`-vs-`aud` accommodation in `OidcBearerScheme`
  (backend) needs confirming against a real token from **this** pool once
  it's live — see `cognito.tf`'s comment.

18	| `aws_secretsmanager_secret.*` (2, infra-owned) + IAM grants | `database-url`/`redis-url` (infra-owned, referenced by ARN in task defs) + the app's own runtime grant under `AWS_SECRETS_MANAGER_PREFIX` (`SECRET_STORE=aws_secrets_manager`) |
19	| `aws_iam_openid_connect_provider.github` + `aws_iam_role.github_deploy` | GitHub Actions → AWS auth for the Deploy workflow, OIDC federation, no stored access keys |
20	| CloudWatch Log Groups (4) | Container logs. No APM/tracing wired up yet — the OTel core is vendor-neutral but the exporter shipped so far is Azure-only |

23	
24	- **OpenTofu** (`tofu`), not Terraform — same ADR 0024 rationale as the Azure stack.
25	- **AWS CLI credentials** for a **scoped IAM user**, never root. This repo's own bring-up used `AWS_PROFILE=dataq-deploy` (set as the default in the operator's shell) — see the session notes for the IAM bootstrap steps (create user, attach a policy, remove root's access keys/login session).
26	- A **GitHub repo** with Actions enabled (for the OIDC federation to have something to trust).
27	- Nothing else pre-exists — this stack creates its own VPC, database, cache, etc. from scratch, unlike the Azure stack's shared-resource dependencies.

31	```bash

33	tofu init

61	## State encryption
62	
63	Same discipline as the Azure stack (`versions.tf`'s `encryption {}` block):
64	the local state holds the generated RDS/ElastiCache passwords in plaintext

    """The response body as a parsed JSON object, or `ValueError`.

    A 200 carrying an HTML error page (a proxy in front of the IdP), a JSON
    scalar (`null`), or an `application/jwt` userinfo body must hit the same
    fail-closed branch as an outage — `json.JSONDecodeError` is NOT an

    `(httpx.HTTPError, ValueError)` and get both shapes.
    """

    if not isinstance(body, dict):
        raise ValueError("expected a JSON object body")

_USERINFO_TTL_SECONDS = 300.0
_USERINFO_CACHE_MAX = 1024
_userinfo_cache: dict[str, tuple[float, dict[str, Any]]] = {}
#: Discovery documents are static per issuer for a process lifetime (the REST
#: scheme resolves once at startup; this is the sync/MCP path's equivalent).
_discovery_cache: dict[str, dict[str, Any]] = {}
#: One lock for both caches: the REST validator mutates them from the event-loop
#: thread while MCP tools (sync `def`s in worker threads) do the same — an
#: unguarded eviction sweep can hit "dict changed size during iteration".
_oidc_cache_lock = threading.Lock()


def _userinfo_cache_get(token: str) -> dict[str, Any] | None:
    with _oidc_cache_lock:
        entry = _userinfo_cache.get(hashlib.sha256(token.encode()).hexdigest())
    if entry is None or entry[0] < time.monotonic():
        return None
    return entry[1]


def _userinfo_cache_put(token: str, claims: dict[str, Any]) -> None:
    now = time.monotonic()
    with _oidc_cache_lock:
        if len(_userinfo_cache) >= _USERINFO_CACHE_MAX:
            for key in [k for k, (expiry, _) in _userinfo_cache.items() if expiry < now]:
                del _userinfo_cache[key]
            while len(_userinfo_cache) >= _USERINFO_CACHE_MAX:
                # Still full after dropping expired entries: evict oldest-inserted.
                del _userinfo_cache[next(iter(_userinfo_cache))]
        _userinfo_cache[hashlib.sha256(token.encode()).hexdigest()] = (
            now + _USERINFO_TTL_SECONDS,
            claims,
        )

    RECOMMENDED, not required — the caller proceeds with whatever the token
    carried). Raises `httpx.HTTPError` on an outage: an unreachable endpoint is
    an outage to surface, never an empty identity (the ADR 0039 decision 6
    lesson applied to auth). The REST path (`OidcBearerScheme._verify`) does
    the same fetch through its own async client; both share the TTL cache.

    the same way `_extract_claims` reads `AzureUser.claims`.

    the near-universal default for GCP Identity Platform/Okta/Auth0/Keycloak)
    signs with RSA; a provider that signs with something else fails closed
    (`_verify` returns `None`, i.e. the standard 401) rather than silently
    accepting an unverified token — extend `_signing_key` if that's ever needed.
    """

        self._issuer = issuer.rstrip("/")
        self._audience = audience
        self._client = httpx.AsyncClient(timeout=timeout)
        self._jwks_uri: str | None = None
        self._jwks_cache: dict[str, Any] | None = None
        self._userinfo_endpoint: str | None = None

        """Resolve discovery endpoints and pre-warm the JWKS cache.

        `azure_scheme.openid_config.load_config()`: a deployment must not report
        healthy while unable to validate a single token.

        only call it synchronously — see its docstring), so it runs off the
        event loop thread here rather than blocking it. `userinfo_endpoint` is

[`deploy/.env.app.prod.example`](.env.app.prod.example) (app settings) +
[`deploy/terraform/azure/variables.tf`](terraform/azure/variables.tf) (infra):

| Setting | Eval default | Production |
|---|---|---|
| `AUTH_DEV_BYPASS` | `true` in the compose file, but **inert by default** — email OTP (`DATAQ_SIGNIN_EMAIL`) wins over it in `auth.py` whenever OTP is configured, which it is out of the box (#1150). It only takes effect once you explicitly clear `DATAQ_SIGNIN_EMAIL` (the documented downgrade). | **`false`** — this is the master auth switch; leaving it on means **no authentication at all**. |
| `AZURE_TENANT_ID` / `AZURE_API_CLIENT_ID` / `AZURE_SPA_CLIENT_ID` | empty | your Azure AD tenant + the two app registrations (API + SPA). |
| **Frontend auth config** | `DATAQ_AUTH_MODE=otp` (eval default — compose sets `${DATAQ_AUTH_MODE:-otp}`) | the **same generic image**, reconfigured at **runtime** — `DATAQ_AUTH_MODE=oidc` + `DATAQ_AUTH_AUTHORITY` / `DATAQ_AUTH_CLIENT_ID` / `DATAQ_AUTH_API_SCOPE` (ADR 0028). **No rebuild** — nginx injects `/config.js` from env. See [frontend/Dockerfile](../frontend/Dockerfile). |
| `SECRET_STORE` | `openbao` (local/eval — ADR 0039) | **`azure_key_vault`** + `AZURE_KEY_VAULT_URL` + the managed identity's `AZURE_CLIENT_ID` (#408). |
| `DATABASE_URL` / `REDIS_URL` | inline, passwordless | Key Vault-backed Container Apps secrets — **never literals**; real credentials. |

9	two are disjoint by prefix, composed in ``_PatOrJwtVerifier``.

1	# DataQ — deployment guide
2	
3	How DataQ v1 is deployed to Azure. Infrastructure is **in-repo OpenTofu**
4	(`deploy/terraform/azure/`, applied — [ADR 0024](../docs/adr/0024-app-deployment-infrastructure.md));
5	the app rolls out via the **`Deploy`** workflow
6	([.github/workflows/deploy.yml](../.github/workflows/deploy.yml), `workflow_dispatch`).
7	The stack is **live** — this is the runbook to provision a fresh environment and to
8	deploy a new image. Related: [ADR 0025](../docs/adr/0025-production-image-pip-slim.md)
9	(slim+pip image), [ADR 0023](../docs/adr/0023-container-image-registry-ghcr.md) (GHCR).
10	
11	Azure is **one** deploy target behind the app's seams (ADR 0010/0013) — the
12	manifests here are infra config, not business logic. No Azure resource names are
13	hardcoded in app code; they live only as OpenTofu vars + workflow `vars`/`secrets`.
14	
15	## Before you deploy: production prerequisites
16	
17	Read this before a production rollout. It's the "what must change, what access you
18	need, and what your cloud must provide" checklist; the [provisioning runbook](#one-time-provisioning)
19	below is the how.
20	
21	### 1. What you must change (never ship the eval/dev defaults)
22	
23	The prebuilt-image quickstart ([docs/getting-started](../docs/getting-started.md)) boots
24	into **email-OTP sign-in by default** (#1150) — a bundled Mailpit catcher stands in for
25	an SMTP relay, uses a passwordless DB, and binds to loopback. Dev-bypass (no
26	authentication at all) is an **explicit two-variable downgrade**
27	(`DATAQ_SIGNIN_EMAIL= DATAQ_AUTH_MODE=bypass`), not the default — and leaving
28	`DATAQ_SIGNIN_EMAIL` unset entirely refuses to start rather than silently picking a
29	mode for you. A production deployment must flip all of the following. Values live in
30	[`deploy/.env.app.prod.example`](.env.app.prod.example) (app settings) +
31	[`deploy/terraform/azure/variables.tf`](terraform/azure/variables.tf) (infra):
32	
33	| Setting | Eval default | Production |
34	|---|---|---|
35	| `AUTH_DEV_BYPASS` | `true` in the compose file, but **inert by default** — email OTP (`DATAQ_SIGNIN_EMAIL`) wins over it in `auth.py` whenever OTP is configured, which it is out of the box (#1150). It only takes effect once you explicitly clear `DATAQ_SIGNIN_EMAIL` (the documented downgrade). | **`false`** — this is the master auth switch; leaving it on means **no authentication at all**. |
36	| `AZURE_TENANT_ID` / `AZURE_API_CLIENT_ID` / `AZURE_SPA_CLIENT_ID` | empty | your Azure AD tenant + the two app registrations (API + SPA). |
37	| **Frontend auth config** | `DATAQ_AUTH_MODE=otp` (eval default — compose sets `${DATAQ_AUTH_MODE:-otp}`) | the **same generic image**, reconfigured at **runtime** — `DATAQ_AUTH_MODE=oidc` + `DATAQ_AUTH_AUTHORITY` / `DATAQ_AUTH_CLIENT_ID` / `DATAQ_AUTH_API_SCOPE` (ADR 0028). **No rebuild** — nginx injects `/config.js` from env. See [frontend/Dockerfile](../frontend/Dockerfile). |
38	| `SECRET_STORE` | `openbao` (local/eval — ADR 0039) | **`azure_key_vault`** + `AZURE_KEY_VAULT_URL` + the managed identity's `AZURE_CLIENT_ID` (#408). |
39	| `DATABASE_URL` / `REDIS_URL` | inline, passwordless | Key Vault-backed Container Apps secrets — **never literals**; real credentials. |
40	| `CORS_ALLOW_ORIGINS` | n/a (same-origin) | empty — the frontend Container App proxies `/api` same-origin (ADR 0028); set the SPA origin only if you split them. |
41	| `PUBLIC_BASE_URL` | n/a | the public origin — used to assemble inbound webhook URLs **and** the "View run" deep links in Slack/email alerts (#416); unset → alerts omit the link. |
42	| `WORKSPACE_ADMIN_EMAILS` | seeded dev user | a **minimal** real allowlist — admins can read every suite's failing-row samples (see [Operational notes](#operational-notes)). |
43	| `RATE_LIMIT_ENABLED` | `true` | keep **`true`** — the fixed-window throttle on every public surface (REST + webhooks + `/mcp`), ADR 0035. Fail-open (a Redis outage disables it, logged); set `false` only to fully disable. |
44	| `RATE_LIMIT_AUTHENTICATED_PER_MINUTE` / `RATE_LIMIT_UNAUTHENTICATED_PER_MINUTE` / `RATE_LIMIT_WEBHOOK_PER_MINUTE` | `300` / `120` / `120` | per-minute caps, keyed per `sha256(bearer)` (authenticated) or client-IP (rest). The webhook cap is **per provider + IP** (#785) — each of adf/airflow/dbt has its own bucket at this cap; the per-IP webhook *total* is `RATE_LIMIT_WEBHOOK_IP_PER_MINUTE`. Defaults are generous; **tighten `RATE_LIMIT_WEBHOOK_PER_MINUTE`** to your orchestrator's real callback cadence. |
45	| `RATE_LIMIT_WEBHOOK_IP_PER_MINUTE` | `240` | per-IP ceiling across **all** webhook buckets from one IP (#785) — bounds the aggregate a single IP can spend by rotating provider segments; without it, per-provider buckets would multiply the per-IP webhook budget. |
46	| `RATE_LIMIT_AUTH_PER_MINUTE` | `10` | strict per-IP cap for `/api/v1/auth/*` (OTP mint/verify, #1127) — checked **before** the bearer branch, so a token can't dodge it. This is the per-IP **backstop**; the tight screw is `AUTH_OTP_REQUEST_PER_EMAIL_PER_10MIN` below. **Tuning note (NAT pools):** per-IP buckets fold onto `RATE_LIMIT_IPV4_PREFIX` (default /24), so an entire corporate-NAT or campus egress range shares these 10 requests/minute — a burst of simultaneous sign-ins from one office can lock the pool out for the window. If your users sign in from behind one egress, **raise this** (30–60 is still a meaningful cap) rather than narrowing the global prefix to /32, which would strip NAT-evasion protection from the `webhook` and `unauth` classes too. The per-email counter is what actually bounds abuse per mailbox, and it is unaffected by NAT. |
47	| `RATE_LIMIT_IP_PER_MINUTE` | `1200` | per-IP ceiling across **all** bearer buckets from one IP — the rotated-token backstop (a client cycling a fresh random `Bearer` per request can't mint unlimited fresh per-token buckets to dodge the cap). Applies only to the `default` (bearer) class; the unauth class is already per-IP, the webhook class has its own ceiling above. |
48	| `RATE_LIMIT_IPV4_PREFIX` / `RATE_LIMIT_IPV6_PREFIX` | `24` / `64` | per-IP buckets key on this address **prefix**, not the full address (#789) — a rotating NAT/proxy pool inside one allocation shares a bucket instead of diluting the cap across sibling /32s. `/32` / `/128` disable grouping; widen or narrow per deployment (a CGNAT-heavy user base may warrant `/32`). |
49	| `RATE_LIMIT_XFF_TRUSTED_HOPS` | `1` | number of trusted proxies that append `X-Forwarded-For` in your deployment — the real client is the entry that many hops from the right. **`1`** for a single-proxy / compose setup (rightmost); **`3`** for the ACA public-envoy→nginx→internal-envoy chain (set in the IaC stack). A chain shorter than this falls back to the socket peer. |
50	| `AUTH_EMAIL_SMTP_HOST` / `_PORT` / `_USERNAME` / `_FROM` / `_PASSWORD_SECRET_NAME` | unset | email OTP sign-in (ADR 0032) — the third authenticator, for deployments with **no IdP**. Set all four (port defaults to 587) to enable the mailer; the password resolves from the SecretStore **by name**. Deliberately separate from the `EMAIL_*` alert mailer, so a misconfigured alert channel can never block sign-in. **A partial block refuses to boot**, naming the missing vars. **Verify it actually works** with the admin SMTP pre-flight test (#737) — `POST /api/v1/admin/auth-email/test` as a workspace admin sends a real message to the caller's own address and, on failure, names the exact transport stage that broke (`connect` / `tls` / `auth` / `send`) in the error envelope's `detail.stage` — catches a misconfigured relay at install time instead of at a teammate's first sign-in attempt. **`/mcp` stays mounted in this mode** (#1128) — but with no IdP there is no bearer token to validate, so a **PAT (`dq_live_…`) is the only credential it accepts**: raw JWTs and session cookies are both rejected. Tell MCP users to mint an API key. |

1	# Getting started
2	
3	Two tracks, matched to why you're here:
4	
5	- **Run / evaluate / self-host** → pull the prebuilt images (below). Recommended.
6	- **Develop / contribute** → build from source with `scripts/setup.sh` ([further down](#develop-from-source)).
7	
8	## Run from prebuilt images (recommended)
9	
10	**Prerequisite:** Docker (Compose v2). No source checkout, no conda, no Node, no Azure
11	tenant.
12	
13	```bash
14	curl -O https://raw.githubusercontent.com/TheurgicDuke771/DataQ/main/docker-compose.ghcr.yml
15	export OPENBAO_TOKEN=$(openssl rand -hex 16)     # root token for the bundled vault
16	export DATAQ_SIGNIN_EMAIL=you@example.com        # the address allowed to sign in
17	docker compose -f docker-compose.ghcr.yml up
18	```
19	
20	This pulls the published images from GHCR and brings up Postgres + Redis + the API +
21	Celery worker + the UI + a local mail catcher, runs migrations, and seeds demo data.
22	Open **`http://localhost:3000`**, type the address you exported, and read the 6-digit
23	code in the bundled inbox at **`http://localhost:8025`**. API + Swagger at
24	`http://localhost:8000/docs`.
25	
26	- **Sign-in works with no SMTP relay.** The stack bundles its own mailbox
27	  ([Mailpit](https://mailpit.axllent.org), MIT), so DataQ's real mailer runs its real
28	  SMTP path and the message lands in a web inbox on your machine instead of the
29	  internet. No mailbox has to exist; nothing leaves the host.
30	- **Multi-arch:** the images are `linux/amd64` + `linux/arm64`, so Apple Silicon runs
31	  native (not emulated).
32	- **Loopback-only:** every port binds to `127.0.0.1` — the stack is reachable from your
33	  own machine but never the LAN. That matters more than usual for `:8025`, which serves
34	  live sign-in codes to anyone who can reach it. **Not for production** — a real deploy
35	  uses the OpenTofu stack (`deploy/terraform/azure`, ADR 0024).
36	- **Pin a release** instead of the moving stable tags:
37	  `DATAQ_BACKEND_TAG=vX.Y.Z DATAQ_FRONTEND_TAG=vX.Y.Z docker compose -f docker-compose.ghcr.yml up`.
38	- **Reset:** `docker compose -f docker-compose.ghcr.yml down -v` (drops the seeded DB).
39	- **Downgrade to no sign-in at all** — deliberate, not a default:
40	  `DATAQ_SIGNIN_EMAIL= DATAQ_AUTH_MODE=bypass docker compose -f docker-compose.ghcr.yml up`.
41	  Every request then resolves to one fixed user and anyone who can reach the port is a
42	  workspace admin. Omitting `DATAQ_SIGNIN_EMAIL` entirely does **not** get you this —
43	  compose stops and names both options, because a permissive auth posture should be a
44	  decision somebody made rather than the one they got by not reading.
45	
46	## Choosing an auth mode
47	
48	DataQ ships **three** ways to log a human in. They are a ladder — pick the rung that
49	fits, but note where the default sits:
50	
51	| Mode | For | You must bring | Sign-in looks like |
52	|---|---|---|---|
53	| **`otp`** ← *the default* | A small team, or anyone evaluating locally | an **SMTP relay** in production — **nothing locally**, the compose stacks bundle a mailbox | you type your address, DataQ emails a 6-digit code, you type it back |
54	| **`oidc`** | An organisation that already has an IdP | an **OIDC app registration** (Azure AD, Okta, Keycloak, Cognito, …) | your normal SSO redirect |
55	| **`bypass`** ← *an explicit downgrade* | Throwaway solo work on a machine only you can reach | nothing | no sign-in at all — every request resolves to one fixed demo user, who is a workspace admin |
56	
57	**`otp` is what you boot into; `bypass` is the explicit downgrade.** Both compose stacks
58	used to start in `bypass`, which meant anyone who could reach the port administered a
59	tool that stores warehouse credentials — and an eval stack's defaults are the security
60	posture people actually run (the same reasoning that moved the default secret store off
61	the plaintext one, ADR [0039](adr/0039-openbao-self-hosted-secret-backend.md)). What made
62	`otp` unusable as a default was the SMTP relay it used to require; the bundled catcher
63	removes that, so the only thing left to supply is *who* is allowed in — one variable,
64	`DATAQ_SIGNIN_EMAIL`, which `scripts/setup.sh` asks for. Setting it empty is the
65	downgrade; leaving it unset stops the stack rather than picking for you.
66	
67	The mode is **never inferred**. Anything unrecognised or half-configured renders an
68	"authentication not configured" banner rather than quietly falling back to something
69	permissive — and the backend refuses to boot on a half-configured OTP block rather than
70	coming up unable to log anybody in.
71	
72	**Two selectors, set them together.** The frontend's `DATAQ_AUTH_MODE` (injected at
73	runtime by nginx — ADR 0028) and the backend's own mode (inferred from its `AZURE_*` or
74	`AUTH_EMAIL_*` settings) are separate contracts, and **neither can derive the other**.
75	Backend OTP on with the frontend on `oidc` shows an SSO flow against an IdP that isn't
76	configured; the reverse shows a code form whose endpoints 503.
77	
78	### `otp` — email one-time codes (ADR [0032](adr/0032-email-otp-signin.md))
79	
80	The default, and the rung for teams that have email but no IdP.
81	
82	**Locally there is nothing to configure but your address.** Both compose stacks run a
83	[Mailpit](https://mailpit.axllent.org) container (MIT) as the mailbox: DataQ performs a
84	real SMTP submission against it — the same `connect → AUTH → send` path a production
85	relay gets — and the message appears in a web inbox at `http://localhost:8025`. The
86	mailer runs with `AUTH_EMAIL_TLS_MODE=none` there, which is the plaintext downgrade
87	`none` exists for and is logged loudly on every send: it is correct against a container
88	you started on your own machine and wrong against anything else.
89	
90	**In production you still bring your own relay** — bundling an outbound mailer is a
91	deliberate non-goal (direct-to-MX from an arbitrary self-hosted IP gets sign-in codes
92	spam-foldered, and a vendor relay would leak sign-in metadata to a third party). Frontend:
93	
94	```
95	DATAQ_AUTH_MODE=otp
96	```
97	
98	Backend — all four mailer values plus **at least one allowlist entry** (there is no open
99	registration; DataQ holds failing-row samples, which are PII):
100	
101	```
102	AUTH_EMAIL_SMTP_HOST=smtp.example.com
103	AUTH_EMAIL_SMTP_PORT=587
104	AUTH_EMAIL_USERNAME=dataq@example.com
105	AUTH_EMAIL_FROM=dataq@example.com
106	AUTH_EMAIL_PASSWORD_SECRET_NAME=dataq-smtp     # the VALUE lives in your secret store
107	AUTH_OTP_ALLOWED_DOMAINS=example.com           # and/or AUTH_OTP_ALLOWED_EMAILS=...
108	WORKSPACE_ADMIN_EMAILS=you@example.com         # bootstrap: your own address
109	```
110	
111	First sign-in: put your own address in **both** the allowlist and `WORKSPACE_ADMIN_EMAILS`,
112	then sign in to your own mailbox. There is no seeded password to rotate.
113	
114	The sign-in form is deliberately credential-only — no sign-up step, no name field, per ADR
115	0032 — so a first-time OTP user's row has no name yet. The app offers a one-time, skippable
116	prompt for one right after that first sign-in (#1139). Skipping it is fine — the name is
117	cosmetic, never an authz input — and it (or any later change) is always available from
118	**Profile**, for every auth mode, not just `otp`.
119

The ALB SG admits CloudFront's origin-facing managed prefix list — shared by ALL distributions — so a third party could point their own distribution at this ALB's discoverable DNS name and reach the origin over plain HTTP through their edge. Standard closure: cloudfront.tf injects a secret custom origin header (e.g. \`X-DataQ-Edge\`, value from \`random_password\` — lives only in encrypted TF state) and the frontend nginx template rejects requests without it (403). Needs a frontend image change (nginx.conf.template + a new runtime env var) + the TF wiring, so it rolls with a normal frontend release." 2>&1 | tail -1

content.content:
Skill "code-review" completed (forked execution).

Result:
All candidate angles are exhausted; the two surviving candidates were verified directly against the live GHCR registry rather than by a vote-agent — the evidence is empirical:

- `dataq-backend:main-a3852cb8…` (last backend-touching main merge) → **200**
- bare `dataq-backend:a3852cb8…` → **404**
- tip of main `43f22a05…` (docs-only commit) → **404** under both tag forms
- `latest` → 200 (proving the probe itself works)

So the PR's central recipe — `image_tag=$(git rev-parse origin/main)`, repeated in all three files — is CONFIRMED broken on two independent mechanisms: publish-images.yml prefixes branch-push tags with `main-` (the bare `:<sha>` is owned solely by the manual-dispatch Azure deploy.yml, per that workflow's own tag-ownership comment), and its `paths` filter skips docs-only merges, so the tip of main frequently has no image at all — as is true right now. Everything else checked out: the `/` health-check path is served 200 by nginx's `try_files $uri /index.html` and the ALB's default matcher is 200; removing the variable defaults breaks no CI caller (no workflow runs AWS tofu); the HCL heredoc is safe (`$(` is not HCL interpolation); the README's env-prefix/backslash bash is now correct (it actually fixes the old broken `\`-before-comment continuation).

```json

  {
    "file": "deploy/terraform/aws/README.md",
```

# the cause nor the fix. It was caught and dispatched by hand within 36 seconds

#
# So: if the compose comes from `main`, the image it names must come from `main`
# too. The `paths` filter keeps the cost off docs-only merges. Pinning a released
# tag in the compose file was the considered alternative and is rejected — it just
# inverts the skew, since a compose edit on `main` would then reference an image
# built before that edit.

  workflow_dispatch:
    inputs:
      tag:
        description: "Extra immutable tag to publish alongside :latest + the commit SHA (e.g. v1.0.0). Blank → just :latest + SHA."
        default: ""

    branches:
      - main

      # adds or renames a setting in the template against a `:latest` whose
      # `Settings` has extra="forbid" and closed Literals reproduces the #1056

# DataQ on AWS — Terraform (OpenTofu) runbook

A second, parallel deployment of DataQ (Azure stays the deployed prod — see
`deploy/terraform/azure/`), into a fresh, dedicated AWS account. Unlike the
Azure stack, nothing here is shared with another stack: this account exists
only for this deployment.

## What it creates

| Resource | Purpose |
|---|---|
| VPC, 2 public subnets, IGW, route table | Networking. No NAT Gateway (decision: public-subnets-no-NAT, ~$33/mo saved — ECS tasks get no public inbound access, only the ALB→frontend path is internet-reachable) |
| `aws_ecs_cluster.app` + 3 Fargate services (api, worker, frontend) + 1 task def (migrate) | The app itself. api is internal-only (Cloud Map DNS `api.dataq.local`); frontend is the sole public surface (behind the ALB); worker runs embedded celery-beat, `desired_count=1` always (cannot scale to zero) |
| `aws_lb.app` (ALB, HTTP-only) | Public ingress → frontend target group only |
| `aws_db_instance.app` (RDS Postgres, `db.t4g.micro`) | The app's own database — this stack creates it directly (no shared-server bootstrap dance like the Azure stack, since this account is dedicated) |
| `aws_elasticache_replication_group.app` (`cache.t4g.micro`, TLS + auth token) | Celery broker + rate-limit store |
| `aws_cognito_user_pool.app` + SPA client | OIDC identity provider, validated by the backend's provider-neutral `OidcBearerScheme` (ADR 0026 amendment) — not Azure AD |
| `aws_secretsmanager_secret.*` (2, infra-owned) + IAM grants | `database-url`/`redis-url` (infra-owned, referenced by ARN in task defs) + the app's own runtime grant under `AWS_SECRETS_MANAGER_PREFIX` (`SECRET_STORE=aws_secrets_manager`) |
| `aws_iam_openid_connect_provider.github` + `aws_iam_role.github_deploy` | GitHub Actions → AWS auth for the Deploy workflow, OIDC federation, no stored access keys |
| CloudWatch Log Groups (4) | Container logs. No APM/tracing wired up yet — the OTel core is vendor-neutral but the exporter shipped so far is Azure-only |

## Prerequisites

- **OpenTofu** (`tofu`), not Terraform — same ADR 0024 rationale as the Azure stack.
- **AWS CLI credentials** for a **scoped IAM user**, never root. This repo's own bring-up used `AWS_PROFILE=dataq-deploy` (set as the default in the operator's shell) — see the session notes for the IAM bootstrap steps (create user, attach a policy, remove root's access keys/login session).
- A **GitHub repo** with Actions enabled (for the OIDC federation to have something to trust).
- Nothing else pre-exists — this stack creates its own VPC, database, cache, etc. from scratch, unlike the Azure stack's shared-resource dependencies.

## Apply

```bash
cd deploy/terraform/aws
tofu init
# state_encryption_passphrase comes from your terraform.tfvars — see
# terraform.tfvars.example. image tags: publish-images.yml pushes backend +
# frontend under every main commit SHA — the services RUN these from the
# first apply, so always pass a current SHA (#1349).
TF_VAR_app_db_password="REDACTED" \
tofu plan -input=false -out=tfplan \
  -var="image_tag=$(git rev-parse origin/main)" \
  -var="frontend_image_tag=$(git rev-parse origin/main)"
tofu apply -input=false tfplan
```

**Cost starts here.** `tofu apply` creates real, billable AWS resources (Fargate, RDS, ElastiCache, ALB). Review the plan before applying. See the root-level deployment plan (in the session that built this stack) for the cost breakdown against the AWS free-tier credit.

## After apply — wire the Deploy workflow

```bash
tofu output -raw github_deploy_role_arn   # → repo secret AWS_DEPLOY_ROLE_ARN
tofu output -raw ecs_cluster_name         # → repo variable ECS_CLUSTER
tofu output -raw frontend_url             # → sanity-check reachability
```

```bash
gh secret set AWS_DEPLOY_ROLE_ARN --body "$(tofu output -raw github_deploy_role_arn)"
gh variable set ECS_CLUSTER --body "$(tofu output -raw ecs_cluster_name)"
gh variable set AWS_REGION --body "$(tofu output -raw -json | jq -r .aws_region.value 2>/dev/null || echo us-east-2)"
```

A companion `.github/workflows/deploy-aws.yml` (not yet built) will use these
to `aws-actions/configure-aws-credentials` via OIDC, then run the same
build→push(GHCR)→migrate(RunTask, poll-to-terminal)→`ecs update-service`
sequence the Azure `deploy.yml` runs, adapted to the AWS CLI equivalents.

## State encryption

Same discipline as the Azure stack (`versions.tf`'s `encryption {}` block):
the local state holds the generated RDS/ElastiCache passwords in plaintext
without it. `state_encryption_passphrase` is a **data-at-rest key**, not a
credential — it cannot be revoked or re-minted, and losing it makes
`terraform.tfstate` permanently unreadable. Keep a second copy off this
machine. A wrong/missing passphrase fails closed
(`cipher: message authentication failed`) without corrupting the file.

## Verify

```bash
# Confirm exactly what got created, tagged for this stack:
aws resourcegroupstaggingapi get-resources \
  --tag-filters Key=Purpose,Values=dataq-app-aws

# Reachability (through the frontend — the sole public surface):
curl -s "$(tofu output -raw frontend_url)/healthz"
```

Then in a browser: sign in through Cognito end-to-end, confirm `/api` and
`/mcp` return 401 unauthenticated without a credential, and run one real
suite against a live datasource to confirm the worker path.

## Known gaps in this pass (deliberately deferred, not silently skipped)

- No custom domain / HTTPS — ALB DNS name, HTTP-only. Add Route53 + ACM + an
  HTTPS listener once a domain is chosen.
- No private-subnet/NAT hardening — see `main.tf`'s decision note.
- No `.github/workflows/deploy-aws.yml` yet — this stack only provisions the
  infra the workflow will drive.
- The Cognito `client_id`-vs-`aud` accommodation in `OidcBearerScheme`
  (backend) needs confirming against a real token from **this** pool once
  it's live — see `cognito.tf`'s comment.

attachment.snippet:
1	# DataQ on AWS — Terraform (OpenTofu) runbook
2	
3	A second, parallel deployment of DataQ (Azure stays the deployed prod — see
4	`deploy/terraform/azure/`), into a fresh, dedicated AWS account. Unlike the
5	Azure stack, nothing here is shared with another stack: this account exists
6	only for this deployment.
7	
8	## What it creates
9	
10	| Resource | Purpose |
11	|---|---|
12	| VPC, 2 public subnets, IGW, route table | Networking. No NAT Gateway (decision: public-subnets-no-NAT, ~$33/mo saved — ECS tasks get no public inbound access, only the ALB→frontend path is internet-reachable) |
13	| `aws_ecs_cluster.app` + 3 Fargate services (api, worker, frontend) + 1 task def (migrate) | The app itself. api is internal-only (Cloud Map DNS `api.dataq.local`); frontend is the sole public surface (behind the ALB); worker runs embedded celery-beat, `desired_count=1` always (cannot scale to zero) |
14	| `aws_cloudfront_distribution.app` → `aws_lb.app` (ALB, HTTP :80) | Public ingress. CloudFront terminates HTTPS on its default `*.cloudfront.net` cert (#1345 — Cognito requires an HTTPS redirect URI); the ALB admits only CloudFront's origin-facing ranges and forwards to the frontend target group |
15	| `aws_db_instance.app` (RDS Postgres, `db.t4g.micro`) | The app's own database — this stack creates it directly (no shared-server bootstrap dance like the Azure stack, since this account is dedicated) |
16	| `aws_elasticache_replication_group.app` (`cache.t4g.micro`, TLS + auth token) | Celery broker + rate-limit store |
17	| `aws_cognito_user_pool.app` + SPA client | OIDC identity provider, validated by the backend's provider-neutral `OidcBearerScheme` (ADR 0026 amendment) — not Azure AD |
18	| `aws_secretsmanager_secret.*` (2, infra-owned) + IAM grants | `database-url`/`redis-url` (infra-owned, referenced by ARN in task defs) + the app's own runtime grant under `AWS_SECRETS_MANAGER_PREFIX` (`SECRET_STORE=aws_secrets_manager`) |
19	| `aws_iam_openid_connect_provider.github` + `aws_iam_role.github_deploy` | GitHub Actions → AWS auth for the Deploy workflow, OIDC federation, no stored access keys |
20	| CloudWatch Log Groups (4) | Container logs. No APM/tracing wired up yet — the OTel core is vendor-neutral but the exporter shipped so far is Azure-only |
21	
22	## Prerequisites
23	
24	- **OpenTofu** (`tofu`), not Terraform — same ADR 0024 rationale as the Azure stack.
25	- **AWS CLI credentials** for a **scoped IAM user**, never root. This repo's own bring-up used `AWS_PROFILE=dataq-deploy` (set as the default in the operator's shell) — see the session notes for the IAM bootstrap steps (create user, attach a policy, remove root's access keys/login session).
26	- A **GitHub repo** with Actions enabled (for the OIDC federation to have something to trust).
27	- Nothing else pre-exists — this stack creates its own VPC, database, cache, etc. from scratch, unlike the Azure stack's shared-resource dependencies.
28	
29	## Apply
30	
31	```bash
32	cd deploy/terraform/aws
33	tofu init
34	# state_encryption_passphrase comes from your terraform.tfvars — see
35	# terraform.tfvars.example.
36	#
37	# Image tags (#1349): the services RUN these images from the first apply.
38	# publish-images.yml tags main merges as `main-<full sha>` (the bare `<sha>`
39	# tag is owned by the manual Azure deploy.yml and usually does NOT exist), and
40	# its `paths` filter skips merges that don't change image content — so use the
41	# last IMAGE-BEARING main commit, not the branch tip, and verify the tag
42	# exists before applying:
43	IMG_SHA=$(git log origin/main -1 --format=%H -- backend frontend pyproject.toml)
44	docker manifest inspect "ghcr.io/theurgicduke771/dataq-backend:main-${IMG_SHA}" > /dev/null  # must succeed
45	TF_VAR_app_db_password="REDACTED" \
46	tofu plan -input=false -out=tfplan \
47	  -var="image_tag=main-${IMG_SHA}" \
48	  -var="frontend_image_tag=main-${IMG_SHA}"
49	tofu apply -input=false tfplan
50	```
51	
52	**Cost starts here.** `tofu apply` creates real, billable AWS resources (Fargate, RDS, ElastiCache, ALB). Review the plan before applying. See the root-level deployment plan (in the session that built this stack) for the cost breakdown against the AWS free-tier credit.
53	
54	## After apply — wire the Deploy workflow
55	
56	```bash
57	tofu output -raw github_deploy_role_arn   # → repo secret AWS_DEPLOY_ROLE_ARN
58	tofu output -raw ecs_cluster_name         # → repo variable ECS_CLUSTER
59	tofu output -raw frontend_url             # → sanity-check reachability
60	```
61	
62	```bash
63	gh secret set AWS_DEPLOY_ROLE_ARN --body "$(tofu output -raw github_deploy_role_arn)"
64	gh variable set ECS_CLUSTER --body "$(tofu output -raw ecs_cluster_name)"
65	gh variable set AWS_REGION --body "$(tofu output -raw -json | jq -r .aws_region.value 2>/dev/null || echo us-east-2)"
66	```
67	
68	A companion `.github/workflows/deploy-aws.yml` (not yet built) will use these
69	to `aws-actions/configure-aws-credentials` via OIDC, then run the same
70	build→push(GHCR)→migrate(RunTask, poll-to-terminal)→`ecs update-service`
71	sequence the Azure `deploy.yml` runs, adapted to the AWS CLI equivalents.
72	
73	## State encryption
74	
75	Same discipline as the Azure stack (`versions.tf`'s `encryption {}` block):
76	the local state holds the generated RDS/ElastiCache passwords in plaintext
77	without it. `state_encryption_passphrase` is a **data-at-rest key**, not a
78	credential — it cannot be revoked or re-minted, and losing it makes
79	`terraform.tfstate` permanently unreadable. Keep a second copy off this
80	machine. A wrong/missing passphrase fails closed
81	(`cipher: message authentication failed`) without corrupting the file.
82	
83	## Verify
84	
85	```bash
86	# Confirm exactly what got created, tagged for this stack:
87	aws resourcegroupstaggingapi get-resources \
88	  --tag-filters Key=Purpose,Values=dataq-app-aws
89	
90	# Reachability (through the frontend — the sole public surface):
91	curl -s "$(tofu output -raw frontend_url)/healthz"
92	```
93	
94	Then in a browser: sign in through Cognito end-to-end, confirm `/api` and
95	`/mcp` return 401 unauthenticated without a credential, and run one real
96	suite against a live datasource to confirm the worker path.
97	
98	## Known gaps in this pass (deliberately deferred, not silently skipped)
99	
100	- No custom domain — the public URL is the CloudFront distribution's own
101	  `*.cloudfront.net` domain (HTTPS, default cert — #1345). Once a domain is
102	  chosen: Route53 + ACM cert + an `aliases` entry on the distribution.
103	- No private-subnet/NAT hardening — see `main.tf`'s decision note.
104	- No `.github/workflows/deploy-aws.yml` yet — this stack only provisions the
105	  infra the workflow will drive.
106	- The Cognito `client_id`-vs-`aud` accommodation in `OidcBearerScheme`
107	  (backend) needs confirming against a real token from **this** pool once
108	  it's live — see `cognito.tf`'s comment.

16	# SG for the frontend's published port.
